titulo: Generation Rent: why young Europeans cannot afford a home

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: Across much of Europe, people in their twenties and early thirties are paying more for less space, staying longer in their parents' homes and postponing the milestones that previous generations took for granted. A home of one's own, once a reasonable expectation for anyone with a steady job, has become a distant prospect for millions. This report looks at how it happened and what, if anything, could reverse it.

On a Saturday morning in a mid-sized Spanish city, a queue forms outside a block of flats before the estate agent has even arrived. Most of the people waiting are under 35. Some have come with printed payslips, others with a letter from a parent offering to act as guarantor. The flat on offer has two small bedrooms, no lift and a rent that would swallow close to half of a typical young worker's salary. By lunchtime, the agent says, it will be gone.

Scenes like this are no longer confined to capitals such as Madrid, Paris or Amsterdam. Across the European Union, the age at which young people leave the family home has crept steadily upwards, and in southern Europe it now sits at around thirty, compared with the early twenties in the Nordic countries. The reasons are partly cultural, but economists increasingly agree that the main driver is far simpler: housing has become too expensive relative to the incomes of the young.

Over the past decade, house prices in the EU have risen considerably faster than wages, and rents have followed a similar, if somewhat gentler, path. In many large cities, average rents have climbed by well over a third in ten years. Meanwhile, the wages of workers at the start of their careers have barely kept pace with inflation. The result is a widening gap: a growing share of young tenants spend more than 40 per cent of their disposable income on housing, the threshold at which statisticians consider the burden to be excessive.

Why has the squeeze become so severe? The most common answer is that Europe has simply not built enough homes. After the financial crisis of 2008, construction collapsed in several countries, Spain and Ireland among them, and it has never fully recovered. At the same time, people have kept moving to the cities where the jobs are. Demand has grown while supply has stagnated, and in a market where a new building can take years to plan and complete, prices have done the adjusting.

Other forces have added fuel to the fire. A decade of very low interest rates made property an attractive investment, drawing in large funds that buy entire buildings to rent out. Short-term holiday lets have removed flats from the residential market in popular tourist areas. And smaller households, with more people living alone, mean that the same population needs more homes than it once did. Each of these factors is hotly debated, but together they have tilted the market against first-time renters and buyers.

For those hoping to buy, the obstacles are even higher. Banks typically lend no more than 80 per cent of a property's value, which means that a buyer must save a deposit of around a fifth of the price, plus taxes and fees. With rents absorbing so much of their income, many young people find it almost impossible to put money aside. The rise in interest rates since 2022 has made matters worse, increasing monthly mortgage payments just as prices remained stubbornly high.

One consequence is a quiet but powerful form of inequality. Young people whose parents own property, or can help with a deposit, still manage to get on the housing ladder; those without family wealth increasingly cannot. Several studies suggest that parental support has become one of the best predictors of whether someone in their thirties owns a home. 'It is no longer about how hard you work,' says a housing researcher at a European university. 'It is about who your parents are.'

The effects go well beyond personal finances. Demographers point out that delays in leaving home are linked to later marriages and lower birth rates, a worrying trend for ageing societies. Employers in expensive cities complain that they struggle to recruit nurses, teachers and young engineers who cannot afford to live nearby. And political scientists have noted that frustration over housing is feeding support for parties on both the left and the right that promise radical change.

Governments have responded in very different ways. Some, including parts of Spain and Germany, have introduced caps on rents in areas declared 'stressed'. Supporters argue that such measures protect tenants from sudden and unaffordable increases; critics warn that they discourage landlords from renting and investors from building, shrinking supply in the long run. The evidence is mixed, and much depends on how the rules are designed and whether they are combined with incentives to build.

Others look to Vienna, often held up as a model. The Austrian capital has invested in public and subsidised housing for a century, and a large share of its residents live in homes owned by the city or by non-profit associations. Rents there remain moderate by the standards of other European capitals. Copying the model, however, is not easy: it requires decades of sustained investment and a large stock of public land, which many cities sold off long ago.

The European Union has also begun to take notice. Housing has traditionally been a national and local matter, but Brussels has recently placed affordability on its agenda, with plans to mobilise investment through the European Investment Bank and to give governments more room to subsidise construction. Whether this will make a visible difference on the ground, and how quickly, remains to be seen.

Back in the queue outside the Spanish flat, a 29-year-old engineer explains that she has been looking for three months. She earns a decent salary and has a stable contract, yet she still shares a flat with two other people. 'My parents bought their first home at my age,' she says, shrugging. 'For us, that sounds like science fiction.' Unless Europe finds a way to build more, and faster, her generation may be the first in decades to live less comfortably than its parents.
titulo_es: Generación alquiler: por qué los jóvenes europeos no pueden permitirse una vivienda
resumen_es: Reportaje sobre la crisis de acceso a la vivienda de los jóvenes europeos: sus causas (falta de construcción, inversión, alquiler turístico, tipos de interés), sus consecuencias sociales y las respuestas políticas, del control de alquileres al modelo de Viena.

ideas_clave.idea: Young Europeans increasingly struggle to find an affordable home, as shown by the crowd of under-35s competing for a small, costly flat in a Spanish city.
Young people now leave their parents' home later, especially in southern Europe, chiefly because housing costs have outgrown their incomes.
Over ten years prices and rents have risen far more than starting salaries, so many young tenants devote an excessive share of their income to housing.
The core cause is insufficient construction since 2008 in the face of growing urban demand, aggravated by cheap credit, institutional investors, tourist rentals and smaller households.
Home ownership is even less accessible because buyers need a large deposit they cannot save, and mortgages have become dearer since 2022.
Access to property increasingly depends on family wealth, which creates a new kind of inequality between young people.
The crisis also has demographic, labour-market and political consequences, from falling birth rates to support for radical parties.
Rent controls, tried in parts of Spain and Germany, protect tenants but may reduce supply, so their results depend on their design.
Vienna's century-old social housing model and new EU initiatives are seen as alternatives, though the former is hard to replicate and the latter's impact is uncertain.
Unless Europe builds more and faster, today's young adults may end up living worse than their parents.

resumen_modelo: The report examines why a growing number of young Europeans can no longer afford a home of their own. Illustrated by a crowd of young applicants competing for a modest flat in a Spanish city, the problem is now widespread: people leave the parental home ever later, particularly in southern Europe, mainly because prices and rents have grown much faster than the salaries of those starting their careers, so that many tenants spend an excessive proportion of their income on accommodation. The principal explanation lies in a chronic shortage of new housing since the 2008 crisis, while demand has kept concentrating in cities; low interest rates, investment funds, holiday lets and smaller households have intensified the pressure. Buying is even harder, since a substantial deposit is required and mortgage costs have risen since 2022. As a result, home ownership increasingly hinges on parental wealth, which deepens inequality, and the situation also weighs on birth rates, recruitment and political moderation. Policy responses vary: rent caps shield tenants but may discourage supply, whereas Vienna's long-standing public housing is admired but difficult to copy, and the EU is only beginning to act. The author concludes that, without a sharp increase in construction, this generation risks being worse off than its parents.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The flat described at the beginning of the report has a lift and three bedrooms.
preguntas.cita: The flat on offer has two small bedrooms, no lift
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que el piso tiene dos dormitorios pequeños y no tiene ascensor. Se han cambiado ambos detalles, así que la afirmación es falsa.

preguntas.pregunta: According to economists, what is the main reason young people leave home later?
opciones: Housing has become too expensive compared with their incomes
A shortage of jobs in large cities
respuestas: Housing has become too expensive compared with their incomes
preguntas.cita: economists increasingly agree that the main driver is far simpler: housing has become too expensive relative to the incomes of the young
preguntas.explicacion: El texto reconoce que hay razones en parte culturales, pero subraya que la causa principal es el precio de la vivienda en relación con los ingresos. El paro y los estudios no se mencionan como causa.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Spending more than 40 per cent of disposable income on housing is regarded as an excessive burden.
preguntas.cita: more than 40 per cent of their disposable income on housing, the threshold at which statisticians consider the burden to be excessive
preguntas.explicacion: El texto presenta el 40 % de la renta disponible como el umbral a partir del cual los estadísticos consideran excesivo el gasto en vivienda. La afirmación es verdadera.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 4 una palabra que signifique «se estancó, dejó de crecer».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'stopped growing or developing'.
preguntas.cita: Demand has grown while supply has stagnated
preguntas.explicacion: «Stagnated» (de «to stagnate») significa estancarse. Se contrapone a «has grown», referido a la demanda.

preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a factor adding pressure to the housing market?
opciones: Large investment funds buying whole buildings
Rising immigration from outside the EU
respuestas: Rising immigration from outside the EU
preguntas.cita: drawing in large funds that buy entire buildings to rent out. Short-term holiday lets have removed flats from the residential market
preguntas.explicacion: El párrafo menciona los fondos de inversión, los alquileres turísticos y los hogares más pequeños, pero no la inmigración. Por eso es la única opción que no aparece.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Banks usually require buyers to provide a deposit of about 20 per cent of the property's price.
preguntas.cita: a buyer must save a deposit of around a fifth of the price, plus taxes and fees
preguntas.explicacion: Si los bancos prestan como máximo el 80 % del valor, el comprador debe aportar alrededor de una quinta parte, es decir, un 20 %. La afirmación es verdadera.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the researcher mean by 'It is about who your parents are'?
respuestas: He means that access to home ownership now depends less on one's own effort or income than on family wealth, because parents who own property or can help with a deposit make the difference.
preguntas.cita: parental support has become one of the best predictors of whether someone in their thirties owns a home
preguntas.explicacion: La frase resume la idea del párrafo: el apoyo económico de los padres se ha convertido en el factor decisivo para comprar vivienda, lo que crea desigualdad entre jóvenes.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Frustration over housing is benefiting only left-wing parties.
preguntas.cita: frustration over housing is feeding support for parties on both the left and the right that promise radical change
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que la frustración favorece a partidos tanto de izquierda como de derecha que prometen cambios radicales, no solo a la izquierda.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Rent caps in Germany have reduced average rents by around ten per cent.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto menciona los topes al alquiler en partes de Alemania y dice que la evidencia es mixta, pero no da ninguna cifra sobre su efecto. Por tanto, no se dice.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 9 una palabra que signifique «topes, límites máximos».
preguntas.cita: have introduced caps on rents in areas declared 'stressed'
preguntas.explicacion: «Caps» son límites máximos; «rent caps» es la expresión habitual para los topes al precio del alquiler.

preguntas.pregunta: Why is Vienna's model difficult for other cities to copy?
opciones: Because Austrian law forbids private landlords
Because it requires long-term investment and plenty of public land
Because its rents are higher than elsewhere
Because the EU does not allow housing subsidies
respuestas: Because it requires long-term investment and plenty of public land
preguntas.cita: it requires decades of sustained investment and a large stock of public land, which many cities sold off long ago
preguntas.explicacion: El texto explica que el modelo exige décadas de inversión y mucho suelo público, que muchas ciudades vendieron. Las rentas de Viena son moderadas, y no se habla de prohibiciones legales ni de la UE.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 11 una palabra que signifique «movilizar, reunir (recursos)».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'to gather and put to use'.
preguntas.cita: with plans to mobilise investment through the European Investment Bank
preguntas.explicacion: «Mobilise» (ortografía británica de «mobilize») significa movilizar o reunir recursos, aquí inversión.

preguntas.pregunta: Why does the author return to the young engineer at the end of the report, and what is the overall conclusion?
respuestas: The engineer shows that even young people with a good salary and stable job cannot afford a home of their own. The conclusion is that, unless Europe builds much more housing, this generation may live less comfortably than its parents.
preguntas.cita: her generation may be the first in decades to live less comfortably than its parents
preguntas.explicacion: El caso individual cierra el reportaje y vuelve a la escena inicial; muestra que el problema afecta incluso a jóvenes con buenos ingresos y sirve para formular la conclusión general.

urban concentration of jobs

ideas: Spaniards leave home at around thirty
sharp rent increases in Madrid, Barcelona and coastal areas
debate on tourist flats and the housing law

tribunal.pregunta: Do you think rent controls are a good solution? Why or why not?
tribunal.pista_es: Dar una opinión matizada con argumentos económicos.
ideas: short-term protection of tenants
risk of lower supply and black market
effect depends on design
should be combined with incentives to build

tribunal.pregunta: From an economic point of view, why does housing supply react so slowly to higher prices?
tribunal.pista_es: Explicar la inelasticidad de la oferta a corto plazo.
ideas: planning and construction take years
land scarcity and zoning rules
construction costs and labour shortages

tribunal.pregunta: How can the housing crisis affect a country's productivity and labour mobility?
tribunal.pista_es: Vincular vivienda con mercado laboral y crecimiento.
ideas: workers cannot move to productive cities
recruitment problems for key workers
less consumption and saving among the young

tribunal.pregunta: Should the European Union have a greater role in housing policy, given that it is mainly a national competence?

EU can finance through the European Investment Bank
state aid rules could be relaxed
risk of one-size-fits-all solutions
